context: Each percentage is a share of all products, not just of its parent bucket. The figure gives price range labels and bucket shares but does not specify the total number of products, currency, or a complete rule for assigning endpoints.
description: Branching arrows below “Product data” show successive subdivisions. Buckets that are not split further remain leaves. The first split gives three price buckets: <100 holds 65%, 100–500 holds 20%, and >500 holds 15%. Since <100 holds 65% of all products, it is split into three more buckets.

The second level divides <100 into <10 with 18%, 10–50 with 35%, and 50–100 with 12%. Their shares add up to 18% + 35% + 12% = 65%. The 10–50 bucket still holds a particularly large share (35%), so it is divided into 10–20 with 13%, 20–35 with 12%, and 35–50 with 10%. Their shares add up to 13% + 12% + 10% = 35%.

“Resulting groups” on the right lists the seven leaf buckets of the recursion tree (see the table). Their shares range from 10% to 20%, much more evenly distributed than the initial 65%, 20%, and 15%. The intermediate 65% and 35% totals belong to parent buckets that were split, so they do not count again in the result.

frames.explanation: The seven leaf shares add up to 100%. Each leaf holds 10% to 20%, so the data is more evenly distributed after splitting. An implementation must complete the range labels with explicit endpoint rules.
frames.title: Recursively split crowded price buckets

summary: First divide the products into three price buckets. Then recursively split the crowded buckets holding 65% and 35% of the data to obtain seven more evenly populated leaf buckets.
title: Recursively split crowded price buckets
